items.name: Rigid water containers
items.need: Taps in tall buildings can run dry as soon as the pumps lose power, so a household needs drinking water already stored inside the apartment.
items.how_to_choose: Water weighs about 8.3 lb per gallon, so pick a size you can actually lift: a 7-gallon can is close to 60 lb full, a 5.5-gallon can close to 50 lb, and a 3.5-gallon brick about 30 lb. Measure the closet floor or the gap under the bed before you buy, and choose narrow or low shapes that tuck away. Spread containers along a wall or across several closets rather than in one tall stack, and keep them upright unless the maker says they can lie on their side. Buy food-grade containers made for drinking water, with a screw cap and a vent.

qty.note: Work it out in three steps: the gallons you want stored, less the gallons you already hold as sealed water, divided by the gallons in one purchased pack and rounded up. Example, two adults for 14 days: 28 gallons to store, 6 already held as sealed jugs, 22 still needed; that is 4 containers of 7 gallons (28 gallons, so 6 to spare). A two-pack is two containers: a WaterBrick two-pack holds 7 gallons, not 3.5, so the same household needs 4 two-packs, which is 8 bricks. The sealed water you bought for the first 3 days counts toward the 14-day target: keep it and add containers for the rest. Do not buy 14 days of containers on top of it.

items.already_own: Camping water jugs you already own are fine if they are food-grade, have only ever held drinking water, close tightly and do not smell of plastic or mold after washing. Clean and sanitize them before filling. Do not press old milk or juice jugs, or anything that has held chemicals or fuel, into service.

safety_notes.text: Store at least 1 gallon of water per person per day for 3 days, and aim for a 2-week supply if you can. Store more for pregnant or sick people, pets and hot weather.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Plan on at least one gallon per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation. In very hot weather the need can double.
safety_notes.source_title: Water

safety_notes.text: Use FDA-approved food-grade water storage containers. If you cannot, pick a container with a tight-closing top, made of durable unbreakable material (not glass), with a narrow neck if possible. Never use a container that has held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: For stored water, use thoroughly washed plastic containers such as soft drink bottles, which are the best choice. Never use a container that has held toxic substances.
safety_notes.source_name: FEMA (archived page, Food and Water in an Emergency)
safety_notes.source_title: Food and Water in an Emergency
safety_notes.research_note: Archived FEMA page. The older FEMA and Red Cross booklet also warns against reusing milk jugs, but its PDF could not be opened on 2026-11-14.

safety_notes.text: To sanitize a container: wash it with soap and rinse well. Mix 1 teaspoon of unscented liquid household chlorine bleach (5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite) in 1 quart of water, pour it in, close the container and shake so the mix touches every inside surface. Wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out, let the container air-dry, then fill with clean water and close it tightly.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Replace tap water you stored yourself every 6 months.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Keep stored water somewhere cool (50 to 70 F), out of direct sunlight and away from gasoline, pesticides and other toxic substances. Label each container 'drinking water' with the date you filled it.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

items.name: Sealed bottled and long-life water
items.need: Factory-sealed water is ready to store the day you buy it and needs no cleaning, filling or treating.
items.how_to_choose: Ordinary supermarket water is the cheapest and works well if you use it and replace it before the date on the bottle. Long-life emergency water costs far more per gallon; what you pay for is a stated multi-year shelf life and tough small packs that suit a grab bag or a shelf you will not check often. For a car-free household, carry weight matters: a gallon jug is about 8.5 lb and a 24-bottle case about 27 lb. Keep sealed water in a cool, dark place off the floor of a sunny room.

qty.note: Enough sealed water for the first 3 days: 1 gallon for each person a day. At two weeks, keep it: it counts toward the 14-day total, and your own containers hold the rest.

items.already_own: Any unopened, commercially bottled water you already have counts. Check that the seal is intact and the date has not passed, then add it to your total.

safety_notes.text: Unopened commercially bottled water is the safest and most reliable emergency water supply. Observe the expiration date on store-bought water.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Keep commercially bottled water sealed in its original container and store it in a cool, dark place.

items.name: Bathtub water bladder
items.need: With a few hours' warning, a bladder turns the bathtub into a sealed tank of 65 to 100 gallons of clean tap water, which matters in tall buildings where the taps stop when the pumps lose power.
items.how_to_choose: A bladder only helps if you fill it while the water is still running, so keep it in the bathroom and practice the steps once without filling it. Check that it fits your tub: a standard tub holds about 60 to 70 gallons, less than the headline number on the box. It is single-use in practice, because it cannot be dried out properly afterwards, and the tub is out of action while it is full. Buy a named brand from the maker or a known retailer and keep the hand pump with it.

qty.note: One per bathtub. No bathtub, no bladder: store more water in containers instead.

items.already_own: A clean bathtub filled directly holds water for flushing and washing, but an open tub is not a clean drinking-water container and a worn plug can leak it away overnight. If you already own a bladder, check that the liner, fill sleeve and pump are all in the box and that it has never been filled.

safety_notes.text: Plan on at least 1 gallon of water per person per day. A filled bathtub bladder can cover a household for many days, but it does not replace water stored in advance, because it only works if you get warning.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: If you are unsure whether stored water is still safe, boil it, or disinfect it with plain unscented bleach by the directions on its own label (U4-10).

safety_notes.text: Use containers made of food-grade material for drinking water, and keep stored water away from toxic substances such as cleaning chemicals kept in the bathroom.

items.name: Collapsible water carriers
items.need: If water is handed out at a street tanker, a hydrant station or a lower floor, someone has to carry it home and up the stairs, and soft carriers take almost no space until that day.
items.how_to_choose: Think in stair-loads, not gallons: 2.5 gallons (10 liters) weighs about 22 lb. On stairs carry one at a time, in one hand or on your back, so that a hand stays on the rail; two at once, one in each hand, is for level ground only. Bags that ride inside a backpack keep both hands free. Thin fold-flat cubes are cheap but crease and wear out; fabric-skinned bags last for years. Sanitize carriers before first use, and treat water from an uncertain source before drinking it.

qty.note: Two per household, a fixed number: two people can each carry one, or one person can make two trips. On stairs carry one at a time and keep a hand on the rail.

items.already_own: A hiking hydration bladder, a camping water cube or clean 2-liter soda bottles in a backpack all work. Check that the caps seal, the seams do not weep when squeezed full, and nothing smells musty after washing.

safety_notes.text: Before use, wash a container with soap, rinse, then sanitize with 1 teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5% to 9%) in 1 quart of water, shaking to wet all inside surfaces for at least 30 seconds before pouring it out.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

items.name: Spigots and pumps for water containers
items.need: A full container is too heavy to tip and pour without spilling, so you need a clean way to draw off a cup at a time.
items.how_to_choose: Match the dispenser to the container, because threads differ. The Aqua-Tainer, this site's Standard container, comes with a spigot and takes Reliance's 70 mm parts and its hand pump. A Rhino-Pak pours from the spout it comes with and does not take the Reliance pump. A WaterBrick needs its own spigot lid, sold separately. With a 7-gallon can, which weighs about 60 lb full, the pump is worth buying: it lets the can stay upright on the floor instead of being lifted onto its side at a counter edge. With a lighter container, a spigot or spout that came with it and works is enough. Keep hands and cups off the spout, and wash and sanitize dispenser parts when you clean the container.

qty.note: One working dispenser for the household, a fixed number. The spigot or spout that came with your container counts; buy a pump only if it fits that container, and keep a spare spigot if you rely on the original.

items.already_own: The spigot or spout that came with your container is enough if it seals and does not drip. Check it is not cracked and that the vent opens. Do not use a siphon or pump that has ever moved fuel or chemicals.

safety_notes.text: Clean and sanitize anything that touches stored drinking water: wash with soap, rinse, then use 1 teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5% to 9%) in 1 quart of water for at least 30 seconds.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

safety_notes.text: Prefer containers with a narrow neck or opening and a tightly closing top, and never use equipment that has held toxic chemicals.

item_flags: Many generic hand siphons and battery transfer pumps are sold for fuel as well as water: use only one sold as food-grade, and never one that has moved fuel.
